R Lab: Generalized Linear Models

STA 631 – Statistical Modeling I

Author

Andrew DiLernia

Once completed, submit a zipped file (.zip) containing two total documents via Blackboard: a .qmd Quarto file and the corresponding HTML document.

In this assignment we will be analyzing data on annual Atlantic hurricane counts, summer North Atlantic sea surface temperatures, and El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) climate phases from 1950 to 2022, compiled from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

For this data, we will be concerned with the variables year, hurricane_count, sea_surface_temperature_f, and enso_state. A data dictionary for this data set is included below.

1

  1. First, import data on Atlantic hurricanes between 1950 and 2022 for this lab from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dilernia/STA631/main/data/hurricanes_data_1950-2022.csv. Modify the enso_state variable to be a factor type with "Neutral" as the first or baseline category, "El Niño" as the second category, and "La Niña" as the third category.
  1. Reproduce the histogram of hurricane_count (using binwidth = 1) as provided below.
  1. Reproduce the scatter plot of hurricane_count by sea_surface_temperature_f with a fitted Poisson loglinear regression curve (method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "poisson"), se = FALSE) as provided below.
  1. Reproduce the side-by-side box plots of hurricane_count by enso_state (using scale_fill_viridis_d()) as provided below.
  1. Reproduce the summary table of descriptive statistics for hurricane_count stratified by enso_state exactly as provided below.

2

3

  1. Give a formal statement of the assumed Poisson loglinear regression model, clearly defining the response variable and all predictor variables in context.

  2. Give a statement of the estimated Poisson loglinear regression model, clearly defining the response variable and all predictor variables in context.

4

  1. Obtain diagnostic plots for the fitted Poisson regression model using methods covered in class.

  2. Assess the assumptions for the Poisson regression model, clearly stating whether or not each assumption is met and citing specific evidence from the obtained output.

5

  1. Provide the value of and interpret the estimated slope for sea_surface_temperature_f in context.

  2. Provide the value of and interpret the estimated coefficient for the indicator variable for El Niño in context.

  3. Provide the value of and interpret the estimated intercept in context. Is it sensible and appropriate to interpret the intercept here, or is it considered extrapolation? Why or why not?

6

  1. Calculate the predicted number of Atlantic hurricanes (\(\hat{\mu}\)) for a season where the average summer North Atlantic sea surface temperature is \(72.5^\circ\text{F}\) and the climate phase is Neutral. Is this considered extrapolation?
  1. Calculate the predicted number of Atlantic hurricanes (\(\hat{\mu}\)) in a year with an average summer North Atlantic sea surface temperature of \(72.5^\circ\text{F}\) during an El Niño climate phase. Is this considered extrapolation?

7

  1. Finally, we will compare four candidate regression models for hurricane_count:
  1. Model 1 (poisson_sst): Poisson GLM (log link) with sea_surface_temperature_f only
  2. Model 2 (poisson_enso): Poisson GLM (log link) with enso_state only
  3. Model 3 (hurr_model): Poisson GLM (log link) with sea_surface_temperature_f and enso_state
  4. Model 4 (nb_model): Negative binomial GLM (log link) with sea_surface_temperature_f and enso_state

Fit the remaining candidate models and reproduce the summary table of BIC values across all four models (rounded to 2 decimal places) exactly as displayed below.

  1. Comparing the three Poisson GLMs (Models 1, 2, and 3), which model is preferred based on BIC?

  2. Based on the BIC values, which model is overall (including the negative binomial model) most preferred for modeling annual hurricane counts?
